introduction: Bahá’u’lláh calls backbiting a grievous error that “quencheth the light of the heart,” and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá treats it as the chief cause of coldness in a community. The readings follow a clear order: what talk about absent people does to trust; the turn to one’s own faults; the practice of looking for what is good in others, with the story of Jesus and the white teeth of the dead dog; what to do when someone else begins (do not listen); and the better uses of speech and time. A letter written for Shoghi Effendi adds that a true report is no excuse. Scripture has said most of this before: Leviticus, the Psalms and Proverbs on the talebearer, the Sermon on the Mount, James on the tongue, the Qur’án’s image of eating a dead brother’s flesh, and the rabbis’ count of three victims. Ben Sira, Hillel, Confucius, the Dhammapada and Shakespeare’s Iago join them. The harder questions come from the Qur’án’s exception for one who has been wronged, Jesus’ “tell him his fault,” Proverbs on open rebuke, Ezekiel’s watchman and Mill on good men who do nothing.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the result of speaking ill of an absent person is that the friends grow indifferent and withdraw. Trace how that happens, step by step, in a community you know.
Jesus looked at the dead dog and praised its teeth. What would it take to make that a habit of attention, and is anything lost by it?
“Even if what is said against another person be true,” it is backbiting. The Qur’án excepts “one who hath been wronged.” Where should a person who has been wronged take the matter?
The readings say: do not listen. Proverbs says an angry countenance drives away a backbiting tongue; the Qur’án gives words to say. What have you seen work without shaming the speaker?
Mill says bad men need only that good men do nothing, and Ezekiel’s watchman must sound the trumpet. How do the readings distinguish silence about a person from inaction about a wrong?

Jesus says, “tell him his fault between thee and him alone,” and Proverbs praises open rebuke. When is a direct word to the person the alternative to backbiting, and when is it another form of fault-finding?

outside.why: “Backbiting quencheth the light of the heart, and extinguisheth the life of the soul.” The rabbis counted its victims: it kills the one who speaks, the one who accepts it when he hears it, and the one about whom it is said.
James: the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity; it defileth the whole body.
“Backbiting is divisive … the leading cause among the friends of a disposition to withdraw.” Proverbs: a whisperer separateth chief friends.
What happens when it stops: where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.

“The story grows, is spread, the circle widens.” The Qur’án on a slander that ran through Medina: ye welcomed it with your tongues, and uttered with your mouths that whereof ye had no knowledge; ye counted it a trifle.
Where the circle can be stopped. Ben Sira: if thou hast heard a word, let it die with thee; and be bold, it will not burst thee.
They “backbite their loved ones behind their backs,” and love has gone from among them. Paul: if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
Some had “secretly begun to speak ill of others.” A psalm in God’s voice: thou sittest and speakest against thy brother. These things hast thou done, and I kept silence.

“How couldst thou forget thine own faults and busy thyself with the faults of others?” Jesus: why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?

“Ascribe not to any soul that which thou wouldst not have ascribed to thee.” Ecclesiastes turns it round for the one talked about: take no heed unto all words that are spoken; thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others.
“Speak no evil, that thou mayest not hear it spoken unto thee.” A psalm: keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile.
The tongue was made for another use. A prayer: set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips.

Backbiting is forbidden in the same breath as murder. Leviticus does the same: thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour.
“What hath been prohibited in the holy Books.” The Qur’án: neither backbite one another. Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother?
“Beware lest ye backbite one another.” A psalm asks who may dwell on God’s hill and answers: he that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour.
“Defile not your tongues with the cursing and reviling of any soul.” James: if any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, this man’s religion is vain.
“Cleanse your tongues from reviling.” The Letter to Titus: to speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle.
Do nothing “which would grieve the hearts.” Paul: let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying.
“The tongue is for mentioning what is good.” Proverbs: there is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.
Before a dead dog, Jesus says, “How white are its teeth!” Paul: whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report, think on these things.
“Observe now how He concealed the fault.” The First Letter of Peter: charity shall cover the multitude of sins.
“Each will praise the other.” Proverbs: he that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
“Fault-finding is the most detestable” of qualities. Paul’s portrait of its opposite: charity thinketh no evil; beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things.

“Concentrate on the good qualities of others.” Confucius gives a use for both kinds of neighbour: when we see men of worth, we should think of equaling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.
“Have a sin-covering eye.” Proverbs: hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins.
“A person who is a liar … censures” lying in others. Paul: wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.
“Man must be pleased with all mankind and displeased with himself.” Hillel: do not judge your fellow man until you have reached his place.
“Why should we be tattlers and busy-bodies?” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s English echoes the First Letter to Timothy: not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.
“Why do we not let people alone?” Paul: study to be quiet, and to do your own business.
“Heedless souls are always seeking faults in others.” The Dhammapada: not the perversities of others, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of.
Evil-speaking can “destroy the foundation of humanity.” Ben Sira: many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue.

It has never been permissible “to speak critically of another, even if they be among the wicked.” The Qur’án makes one exception: Allah loveth not the utterance of harsh speech save by one who hath been wronged. To whom, in a Bahá’í community, may a wronged person speak, and what keeps that from being backbiting?
Never “a word or hint that is unworthy about any of the friends.” James: speak not evil one of another, brethren.
“You must not listen.” Proverbs on what a listener’s face can do: the north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue.
Words for excusing oneself. The Qur’án supplied some: wherefor, when ye heard it, said ye not: It is not for us to speak of this?

When people come complaining of each other, “don’t listen to them.” Ben Sira adds what to do with what has already been heard: admonish a friend, it may be he hath not done it; believe not every tale.
“A silent tongue is the safest.” Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel: all my days I grew up among the sages, and I have found nothing better for a person than silence.
Proverbs: in the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.

They speak “of what they have not seen” and mention “what they have not heard.” The Qur’án: follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge; the hearing and the sight and the heart, of each of these it will be asked.
Speaking of what one has not seen is an old offence. The law of Moses: thou shalt not raise a false report.

“How then could it be that the friends of God would plot against you?” Suspicion feeds itself. Iago, as he sets to work on Othello: trifles light as air are to the jealous confirmations strong as proofs of holy writ.

Of bad people: “have nothing to do with them. Do not gossip about them.” John Stuart Mill warned what silence can cost: bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing. Where do the readings place the duty to act against wrongdoing, if not in talk?

“Your very silence should be blame itself.” Ezekiel’s watchman is held guilty if he sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet. What is the difference between warning those who are in danger and gossiping about the one who endangers them?
“People speak too much because they seek fame.” Polonius to his son: give thy thoughts no tongue; give every man thy ear, but few thy voice.
“Time passes in vain talk.” Jesus: every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.

“Even if what is said against another person be true,” it is forbidden. What is taken, in Iago’s own words: he that filches from me my good name robs me of that which not enriches him, and makes me poor indeed.

Faults are not to be discussed in a person’s absence. Jesus gives the other path: if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone. When is that the right course, and when would the readings counsel saying nothing at all?

The teaching is strict even about true statements. Proverbs values frankness to a person’s face: open rebuke is better than secret love; faithful are the wounds of a friend. Does the ban on backbiting leave room for this, and how do the two differ?
The ploughman who keeps his eye on his own furrow. Plato’s short definition of justice in the Republic: doing one’s own business, and not being a busybody.
“Make mention of the servants with good.” The Qur’án: O ye who believe! Guard your duty to Allah, and speak words straight to the point.

proverbs-where-no-talebearer-strife-ceas.text: Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth. As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife. The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly

proverbs-whisperer-separateth-chief-frie.text: A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends

proverbs-multitude-of-words.text: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise

proverbs-debate-thy-cause-with-thy-neigh.text: Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another: Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away

proverbs-angry-countenance-a-backbiting-.text: The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue

leviticus-not-go-up-and-down-as-a-talebe.text: Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour; I am the Lord. Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him

psalm-set-a-watch-before-my-mouth.text: Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips

psalm-speakest-against-thy-brother.text: Thou givest thy mouth to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit. Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother's son. These things hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself: but I will reprove thee, and set them in order before thine eyes

ecclesiastes-thou-thyself-hast-cursed-ot.text: Also take no heed unto all words that are spoken; lest thou hear thy servant curse thee: For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others

james-bridleth-not-his-tongue.text: If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain

timothy-tattlers-also-and-busybodies.text: And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not

romans-wherein-thou-judgest-another.text: Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things

proverbs-open-rebuke-better-than-secret-.text: Open rebuke is better than secret love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful

luke-condemn-not.text: Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven

quran-it-is-not-for-us-to-speak-of-this.text: Wherefor, when ye heard it, said ye not: It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to Thee (O Allah)! This is awful calumny.

quran-harsh-speech-save-by-one-wronged.text: Allah loveth not the utterance of harsh speech save by one who hath been wronged. Allah is ever Hearer, Knower.

quran-received-it-with-your-tongues.text: When ye welcomed it with your tongues, and uttered with your mouths that whereof ye had no knowledge, ye counted it a trifle. In the sight of Allah it is very great.

sirach-let-it-die-with-thee.text: If thou hast heard a word, let it die with thee; and be bold, it will not burst thee

shakespeare-shalt-not-escape-calumny.text: be thou as chaste as ice, as pure as snow, thou shalt not escape calumny
shakespeare-shalt-not-escape-calumny.author: William Shakespeare

avot-nothing-better-than-silence.text: all my days I grew up among the sages, and I have found nothing better for a person than silence

sirach-stroke-of-the-tongue-breaketh-the.text: The stroke of the whip maketh marks in the flesh: but the stroke of the tongue breaketh the bones. Many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue

sirach-admonish-a-friend-it-may-be-he-ha.text: Admonish a friend, it may be he hath not done it: and if he have done it, that he do it no more. Admonish thy friend, it may be he hath not said it: and if he have, that he speak it not again. Admonish a friend: for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale

talmud-malicious-speech-kills-three.text: Third speech, i.e., malicious speech about a third party, kills three people. It kills the one who speaks malicious speech, and the one who accepts the malicious speech when he hears it, and the one about whom the malicious speech is said
